Yep, this is the biggest one. Schools have turned scientists into revenue sources, with tenure and degrees being granted based on the ability to bring research / grant funding to the school. This is one of the reasons that fraudulent journal submissions have increased 10x in the last two decades. Everyone is so desperate to write papers with some 'sensational' finding to attract money to their research. Scientists have gotten so caught up in the play politics for grant money game that objectivity in many major fields of science is seriously in doubt. The only scientists that can really be trusted are those that have already retired - especially in politically charged fields of study.

I'm likely older than most of you. If you had told me when I graduated high school in 1965, that by 2015 my Canadian government would have responded to scientific data that showed rising pollution levels by closing the measuring stations, I would have said it would be impossible.

Likewise the idea that any scientist working for the Federal Government of Canada would be muzzled, forbidden to speak publicly, required to route all inquiries through a government spin-doctoring agency; nope, would not have believed it.

The kind of respect there was for science in the 1960's makes me think of a Norman Rockwell painting; quaint, simple, unadorned. Not so any more. The issues have been drawn so fine, the squabbles are so infantile, the paid shills have muddied everything, the idea of integrity has flown so far out the window, that I'm not sure how the original reputation for pure truthseeking could be recovered.

At one time, a Ph.D was awarded on the basis that a jury agreed you had substantially added to the body of human knowledge. Not sure what the criteria are now, but I doubt that's the main base any more.

And the wilful obtuseness we see nowadays is astonishing. To someone who grew up believing that the whole thrust of human scientific and social development was to escape that kind of "My ignorance is as good as your knowledge" thing that Isaac Asimov spoke about, modern science and its audience, taken together, leave your jaw half open and one finger raised, stalled at the top of a breath.

OP, your idea of making science ever more acceptable is to be applauded. But I put it to you that there is still going to be resistance; I've had several occasions over the years when people I've known have been very frustrated, feeling that if they could just make themselves clear in their explanation, that the other party/side of the argument would see reason. Don't you believe it. My response in these cases is to say to the proposer, "You think this is a conversation, don't you? But it's not."

So my reply to your question is this: the greatest barrier to modern science is the growing body of people who don't care what you have to say, they insist they are right in the face of compelling evidence to the contrary. How do you reach these people? You don't. We have to find some way to live with that.

I'd like to think I can offer you some hope on that front; several universities across the UK are now including Science Communication modules in their courses to help combat what has become the age of information abundance and wilful ignorance. My uni has even gone so far as to have a Professor of Geoscience Communication now.

Hopefully as the next generation of scientists come through people will become more receptive to facts.
